name: Plugins and MIME types
plain: Lists installed plugins and supported MIME types.
meaning: Once a strong fingerprint. Since Chrome 94 the list is a fixed set of PDF viewers, so it now adds little.

limits.headline: Can list your browser plugins and file types, which now adds little
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads
can: List the PDF viewers your browser has
List the file types it can open
Use that list as one small trait of your browser
cannot: List other plugins, since modern browsers show a fixed set
Tell you apart on its own, since most people share the same list
limits.differs: Since Chrome 94 the list is a fixed set of PDF viewers, so almost every Chrome user looks the same.

story.what_it_is: A script lists installed plugins and file types your browser can open. Modern browsers return mostly a fixed list.
story.for_you: You never see it. In the past this list showed old add ons like Flash and PDF viewers and was very unique. Now most browsers show a short fixed list, so it reveals far less.
story.for_makers: Years ago, plugin lists were a top fingerprint. Browsers have since standardized the answer. Bot detectors still use it, because an empty list is a sign of a headless script.

use_cases.example: A bot detector sees an empty plugin list, which real desktop browsers do not have, and raises the risk score.
A site checks whether the browser can show a PDF inline or needs to offer a download.
An older ad script still adds the plugin list to its device ID, though it adds little now.
Old browser games needed plugins like Flash. Today they run through standard browser features instead.
A company portal checks for a PDF viewer before it opens a contract inline.
A visitor counting tool splits traffic by browser family using the plugin list as one clue.
A school site checks that the browser can open the assignment file type before loading it.
